title: Active transport

blocks.heading: Key points
blocks.text:
| Learn | |
|---|---|
| Active transport | particles move against a concentration gradient, using energy from respiration, through carrier proteins |
| Where it matters | ions into root hairs; glucose into villus cells; glucose reabsorbed in kidney tubules |
| What stops it | anything that stops respiration, such as no oxygen in waterlogged soil |
| Diffusion and osmosis | down a gradient, no energy from respiration |

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What active transport is, how carrier proteins do it, and why root hair cells, the villi and the kidney tubules depend on it.

blocks.heading: Active transport
blocks.text: Active transport is the movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration using energy from respiration.

blocks.heading: How carrier proteins move particles
blocks.text: Active transport is done by carrier proteins in the cell membrane. A particle binds to a carrier protein that fits it, on one side of the membrane. The carrier changes shape and moves the particle across, releasing it on the other side. The energy for this comes from respiration: some carriers use it directly, others use it indirectly, but either way active transport stops when respiration stops. Cells that do a lot of active transport contain many mitochondria, which release this energy.

blocks.heading: Root hair cells
blocks.text: Mineral ions such as nitrate are often more concentrated inside root hair cells than in the soil water around them. Diffusion would carry them out, not in, so root hair cells take them in against the concentration gradient by active transport. This needs energy from respiration, so roots need oxygen. In waterlogged soil, which holds little oxygen, the roots take up fewer ions, and crops can show signs of mineral deficiency.

blocks.heading: The villi and the kidney tubules
blocks.text: Epithelial cells of the villi in the small intestine take in glucose by active transport. Glucose can then be absorbed even when there is less of it in the gut than in the cells, so little is left to be lost. Cells lining the kidney tubules reabsorb glucose in the same way, returning it to the blood so that it is not lost in the urine.

blocks.heading: Three ways across a membrane
blocks.text:
The table sets the three processes side by side.

| | Diffusion | Osmosis | Active transport |
|---|---|---|---|
| What moves | particles of a gas or solute | water molecules | particles such as ions or glucose |
| Direction | down a concentration gradient | from a dilute to a more concentrated solution | against a concentration gradient |
| Energy from respiration | not needed | not needed | needed |
| Proteins in the membrane | none needed for simple diffusion | water also passes through water channel proteins | carrier proteins needed |

A quick test: ask which way the particles go compared with their gradient. Down the gradient, the cell spends no energy from respiration. Against the gradient, it must.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: A concentration gradient, and diffusion down one, are explained in Diffusion (3.3.1). Mitochondria and their job are in Cell structure (3.2). Root hairs return in Transport in plants (3.7), the villi in Absorption (3.6.2.4), and the kidney in Excretion in humans (3.11).

blocks.heading: Not every movement needs energy
blocks.text: Only active transport needs energy from respiration, because it moves particles against a concentration gradient. Diffusion and osmosis move particles down a gradient, from where there are more to where there are fewer, and need no energy from respiration.
